brief.head: Being right matters
brief.text: Ajay Shah has no interest in solidarity or being in a gang. What matters, he said, is the minor matter of being correct: forecasting what an intervention will do. {107-C04}

brief.head: Power keeps itself
brief.text: Asked by Ajay Shah why state ownership ends in one-party rule, Amit Varma, thinking aloud, said power seized by coercion is kept by coercion. {107-C16}

brief.head: Woke, then and now
brief.text: ‘Woke’ once meant awake to social injustice, a sense Amit Varma embraces. As an ideology, he argued, it succeeds Marxism: “wokeism begins where liberalism ends.” {107-C23}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the labels we hurl
lead.head: Lifting the fog of the isms
body: Liberal, conservative, socialist, nationalist, left, right: the labels are hurled around daily, and they mean different things to different people. On popular demand, Amit Varma and Ajay Shah set out to define them.
Shah promised listeners “a beautiful storyline”. Varma replied that there was one way in which Shah was like a socialist: “you promise a lot.”
They would be as neutral as they could, they said, though neither uses any of these labels now. Labels, they warned, are dangerous.
## Three warnings

First, separate the common noun from the proper noun: a word’s dictionary meaning is one thing, the baggage a label acquires another. “I know many nationalists who in my view are anti-national,” Varma said. {107-C01}
Second, labels move. ‘Liberal’ in Europe today means almost the opposite of what it means in the US.

Third, labels come with tribes. People who join one adopt all its dogmas and follow it wherever it drifts, as so many American conservatives and libertarians followed Trump. Varma saw the same, to a different extent, in India.
Hence Varma’s fifth law: “All labels that bestow any kind of prestige or virtue upon the bearer eventually come to mean the opposite, as grifters and opportunists outnumber the believers.” {107-C02}
Did Shah know the first four laws? “No, not even one.” Nor, Varma admitted, did he.
Shah added that an idea is not responsible for the person who believes in it: if Trump believes something, that says nothing about whether it is true.
## What they believe

Before defining anything, Varma set out the two hosts’ shared beliefs. The world is positive-sum. Top-down design fails at the scale of a society. Actions must be judged by outcomes, not intentions. And freedom is good in itself and delivers the best outcomes, so think in terms of individuals, not groups.

Shah’s illustration of outcomes over intentions was Adolf Hitler: “if your objective was the glory and furtherance of the Germanic peoples, of German DNA, then there was no bigger disaster for that than the man who espoused this the most.” {107-C05}
## From Locke to Kling

Then came the labels, one by one. Liberalism, Varma said, begins with John Locke’s idea that we own ourselves. Conservatism, in its sophisticated form, begins with Edmund Burke’s warning that means matter.
Marxism, socialism and communism are a theory, a path and a destination. Statism is less an ideology than an attitude: that society can be run from the top.
Varma quoted David Boaz: conservatives want to be your daddy, liberals want to be your mommy, and libertarians want to treat you as an adult.

Left and right began as seating in the French National Assembly. In India, Varma said, they make no sense: “All our parties are left of centre when it comes to economics and right of center in a bad way when it comes to society.” {107-C19}
He closed with Arnold Kling’s *The Three Languages of Politics*. Progressives argue from equality, libertarians from freedom and conservatives from tradition, so they talk past each other. {107-C24}
The way out is to grant the other side’s values. If both of you want less poverty, argue from history and evidence about what will deliver it, and minds can change.
Better still, Varma advised, don’t pin labels on the other person at all: “Instead talk about principles, talk about values.”

second.label: The man of system
second.head: Sparrows out, locusts in
second.deck: Amit Varma’s classic illustration of what top-down planning can do
body: In 1958 farmers in China complained that sparrows were bothering them. Chairman Mao decided that all sparrows should be put to death, and wherever they could be caught across China, they were killed. {#sparrows}

But sparrows ate locusts, Amit Varma said. Once the sparrows died out, the locusts proliferated and destroyed China’s crops. A great famine followed in which forty-five million people died, in what is known as the Great Leap Forward. {107-S01}

For Varma it is the classic illustration of Adam Smith’s “man of system”, who imagines he can arrange people like pieces on a chessboard. Society is too complex for that, he said. Respect the complexity, and don’t meddle too much.

quote.text: When the sparrows died out, the locusts proliferated and they destroyed all the crops of China.

second.caption: Mao’s war on sparrows

third.head: Tiki-taka was a taunt
body: Tiki-taka is now the name for Pep Guardiola’s possession football, which comes from Johan Cruyff’s Total Football. But Guardiola hates the term, Amit Varma said. He didn’t coin it. {107-S06}

The broadcaster Andrés Montes first used it during the 2006 World Cup, before Guardiola was a coach, to describe Spain’s pointless passing. Javier Clemente, the coach of Athletic Bilbao, used it the same dismissive way. Only later did it attach itself to Barcelona.
Varma’s point was about politics. ‘Liberal’ began as a pejorative, and ‘conservative’ was first used as a cuss word against Edmund Burke, who did not coin it either.

Philosophical geniuses, Varma said, are denigrated and kicked about, in economics as in football. “Friedrich Hayek, Milton Friedman, Pep Guardiola, these are all geniuses,” he said, “and we should respect and venerate them.” {107-J12}
third.caption: how tiki-taka began as an insult

p2.title: Say what you mean
p2.deck: Liberal to nationalist: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah define the labels, and say where they stand

sections.label: Liberal
sections.head: Liberal with the definitions
sections.caption: the great liberal paradox
body: ‘Liberal’ comes from the Latin *liber* or *liberalis*, meaning generous and befitting a free person, Amit Varma said. Hence a man who gives too freely is “liberal with his wealth”. {107-J14}

The father of liberalism, he said, is John Locke, whose foundational right is self-ownership. From it follow the rights to life, free speech and property. Isaiah Berlin later called these negative rights.

Mary Wollstonecraft, one of Varma’s great heroes, read Locke at the end of the 18th century and drew the next conclusion: if all of us have these rights, women have them too. Modern feminism, he said, grew out of that. {107-S08}
## A necessary evil

Rights need someone to enforce them. Hence the state, which Thomas Paine, in *Common Sense*, called a necessary evil. It is evil, Varma said, because it holds a monopoly on violence and lives on coerced taxes: to protect our rights, we must give up some of them. {107-C07}
Every ideology, in his view, is really an argument about how much state violence is justified.

Europe kept the older meaning of liberal. In 20th-century America, liberals took up positive rights, like a right to food, and the night-watchman state became an all-encompassing *maibaap* that had to feed you and clothe you. {107-C08}
~ When ‘liberal’ changed in America, Ajay Shah suggested, the small-state people called themselves libertarian, and Varma agreed. Most libertarians, he said, are really just classical liberals.

quote.text: I call it the great liberal paradox, that for our rights to have meaning we must give up some of them

sections.label: Conservative
sections.head: Conserve what, exactly?
sections.caption: Burke and why means matter
body: ‘Conservative’ comes from the Latin for conserve or preserve, Amit Varma said, which raises the question: conserve what? A monarchy, Christian family values, even free enterprise against the welfare state.

The serious philosophy, for him, comes from Edmund Burke, whose *Reflections on the Revolution in France* granted the revolution its fine intentions and warned that its means were all wrong. {107-R14}
Institutions and norms, Varma said, “have gone through natural selection, they’ve passed the test of time”. Change the world by all means, but you cannot burn everything to the ground. {107-C10}
## Two impulses

Ajay Shah separated two impulses in the word. One preserves an established order: religion, family, a social structure, an oligarchy. The other respects the complexity of the world, mistrusts grand schemes and holds that means matter. {107-C09}
Varma rejected the first, because the world needs radical change, and signed on completely to the second.
His heroes of the freedom struggle were the moderates, such as Dadabhai Naoroji and Gopal Krishna Gokhale: liberal in their ends, conservative in their means. {107-S05}
~ India, he argued, has little Burkean conservatism. Much of what goes by the name preserves the past for its own sake, or is a radical tribalism at odds with India’s assimilative traditions.

quote.text: It’s a respect for the richness and complexity of the world. It’s a mistrust of any grand scheme.

sections.label: Marxism
sections.head: Great idea, wrong species
sections.caption: theory, path and destination
body: Marxism, socialism and communism belong together but mean subtly different things. “You can think of Marxism as a theory, socialism as a path, communism as a destination,” Amit Varma said. {107-C11}

From the *Communist Manifesto* of 1848 and *Das Kapital* of 1867 came a world of two classes: a bourgeoisie owning the means of production and a proletariat it exploits. Revolution would bring a dictatorship of the proletariat.
Such a theory seems to explain everything, which is why it seduces the young. At eighteen Varma carried *Das Kapital* in his college bag for a few days, feeling cool and intellectual. {107-S09}
## Five charges

It reduces everything to class, said Max Weber and Karl Popper. Capitalism never collapsed, said Popper and Fukuyama. It ignores race and gender, said Michel Foucault and intersectional thinkers, and in India, Varma added, caste. It defies human nature, said Isaiah Berlin. And it needs mass violence, said Hannah Arendt and Raymond Aron.
The biologist E.O. Wilson put it as “Great idea, wrong species”: it would work for ants. {107-J03}
Ajay Shah offered a Soviet joke. You must break eggs to make an omelette, ran the excuse, until someone asked: “We broke a lot of eggs. Where’s the omelette?” {107-J04}
~ Booms and busts are normal, Shah said, and small beside the compounding of growth: “when you correctly draw the graph, the fluctuations appear irrelevant.” {107-C13}

quote.text: any ideological theory that works will appear to explain everything and therefore is deeply seductive to the young.

sections.label: Socialism
sections.head: Good for society? Not quite
sections.caption: what ‘socialist’ really means
body: In India, Amit Varma said, socialism is used almost benignly, as if it meant whatever is good for society. In political science it means something specific.
He gave four features: public ownership of resources, redistribution to bring about equal outcomes, a planned economy, and fine intentions that socialism never achieves.
Jawaharlal Nehru, under the sway of the Fabian Society he encountered in England, was a Fabian socialist, and India got its five-year plans. {107-J18}
## The wrong preamble

Varma opposed the CAA, which he called monstrous, and was delighted to see young people march holding the Preamble. But many carried the amended text with ‘socialist’ in it, not Ambedkar’s original. {107-S03}
“Socialist doesn’t mean what is good for society,” he said. “Socialism kept us poor for decades longer than necessary.” {107-C15}
Ajay Shah had pointed out that the Hindi *samajwad* carries none of the baggage of public ownership: it broadly means on the side of society. In that sense, Varma said, he is one.
Shah wished Ambedkar, in keeping ‘socialist’ out, had added that the only way to make a socialism is to crush individual rights, which cannot go with constitutional liberal democracy.
~ Varma objected on Ambedkar’s behalf. History had not played out, the Soviet Union still seemed a success, and caste, a visceral evil, occupied his attention.

quote.text: many of them were holding the wrong preamble. They were not holding Ambedkar’s preamble, they were holding Indira’s preamble

sections.label: Nationalism
sections.head: Anti-national, by Varma’s law
sections.caption: patriots and nationalists
body: Both hosts love their country deeply and hate nationalism deeply, Amit Varma said. Patriotism is loving your country. Nationalism defines a nation by othering some people, playing on tribal instincts hardwired into us.

He cited Tagore, who called nationalism a great menace, and Karl Popper, who wrote in *The Open Society and Its Enemies* that it appeals to our tribal instincts, “to passion and to prejudice”. {107-R15}

Savarkar’s *What is Hindutva*, which Varma dated to 1925, defined a Hindu as someone whose homeland and land of worship are both India. That takes in Jains and Buddhists and shuts out Muslims and Christians. Varma called it masterful and deeply toxic. {107-C21}
## Varma’s sixth law
Varma quoted Ramachandra Guha: a patriot strives for a less violent, less poor, less exploitative country, while “a nationalist wants to bomb everybody else”. {107-C20}
Hence his proposed sixth law: anyone who calls others anti-national is the true anti-national.

Ajay Shah admired how Tagore, Gandhi and Nehru were Indian and open to the world at once; Gandhi, he noted, read the New Testament with great interest. Nationalism in India, Shah said, stems from deep insecurity. {107-C22}
~ Nitin Pai, whom both hosts admire, argues for liberal nationalism. Varma, who argued against it at length with Pai on his show, allows that he may be wrong.

quote.text: If you’re actually strong, if you’re actually capable, then you will relax, then you will engage with others as equals

side.boxText: Amit Varma read Adam Smith aloud twice: on the “man of system”, and on how “peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice” carry a state to opulence. Smith, he said, probably first used ‘liberal’ politically. {107-J16}

contQuote.text: I know many liberals who are not liberal. I know many progressive people who espouse policies that would actually set us back and not take us forward. I know many conservatives who hold radical views

stories.caption: Ambedkar’s original preamble
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the word Ambedkar kept out of the Preamble
stories.head: Not in my preamble
body: In 1948, as the Constituent Assembly debated the Preamble, K.T. Shah moved to add three words to it. B.R. Ambedkar rejected two of them: ‘secular’ and ‘socialist’.
His objection to ‘secular’, Amit Varma said, was not to secularism. It was written into every article of the Constitution already, so spelling it out was unnecessary.

On ‘socialist’, Varma read out Ambedkar’s speech to the Assembly. A constitution, Ambedkar said, “is merely a mechanism for the purpose of regulating the work of the various organs of the state”. {#ambedkarspeech}

How society should be organised, he said, must be decided by the people themselves according to time and circumstances. To fix it in the Constitution would be “destroying democracy altogether”. Thinking people might one day devise something better than the socialist organisation of today or tomorrow.
The words went in anyway, added by Indira Gandhi in the mid-1970s. Today, Varma said, any political party that registers in India must pledge allegiance to socialism.

Not that he and Ajay Shah plan a party, which, he said, “of course we never will, because we are thinkers and not doers”. Then he corrected himself: “No, we are doers but in a different way.” {107-J08}
If they did, Varma said, they would have to pledge to socialism, “which fundamentally goes against everything we believe in”. {107-S02}

~ S.V. Raju, the late president of the Swatantra Party, fought the rule in court for many years, arguing that a party that stood against socialism could not pledge allegiance to it. It was, Varma said, a losing battle.
stories.why: A constitution, Ambedkar argued, should regulate the organs of the state and leave the people free to choose how society is organised. Writing in one ideology took that choice away, and still decides who may enter politics.
stories.postscript: Ambedkar’s collected writings, sixty-plus volumes, and Gandhi’s ninety-nine are free online. “This stuff is free,” Varma said. {#ninetynine}

stories.caption: Burke’s postcard to Robespierre
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s invented correspondence, built from real quotes
stories.head: Bro, I warned you
body: In 1790, with the French Revolution under way, Edmund Burke wrote *Reflections on the Revolution in France*. {#burke} He did not quarrel with its ideals of liberty, equality and fraternity. He warned that its means were disastrous.

For the History of Ideas webinar in their Life Lessons course, Amit Varma made up postcards between Burke and Robespierre, one of the notable figures behind the revolution, built from the men’s real quotes.

In the first, Robespierre tells Burke, roughly, to shut up, calls him an old fogey and asks what he is even trying to conserve. Burke’s reply: “Bro, I warned you, I hope you’re around to read this.” {107-S04}
~ Robespierre was not. He had himself been purged, Varma said, after doing a fair amount of purging.
stories.why: Ends and means are separate questions. Change the world by all means, Varma argued, but institutions and norms that have passed the test of time exist for a reason, and you cannot simply burn them to the ground. {107-C10}

stories.caption: land, wealth and the old order
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how land lost its hold on Indian wealth
stories.head: Ploughed under by Infosys
body: Think of the word land in India in 1907 or 1947, Ajay Shah said, and the primal emotions around it. Land meant wealth and income, and the game was to own more of it.
“A person with fifty thousand acres was a bigger person than a person with 10,000 acres,” he said. {107-S07}
Today’s India makes its wealth from business: you build Infosys, you build Reliance Industries. Land is nice to have, but neither necessary nor sufficient to be rich, successful and important.

~ Thinkers from Adam Smith to Karl Marx, Shah said, saw capitalism and globalisation as a wild west wind that would tear up the feudal order. {107-R16} Those who did well from land, aristocracy, religion and family wanted the old order kept, which is how ‘conservative’ came to stand against ‘liberal’.

quote.text: The wealth of today’s India is not created out of land.

stories.start: Neoliberal is a pure cuss word used against people who are for markets
stories.end: I live in the real world. Let's talk about that
stories.caption: the guest who couldn’t define ‘neoliberal’
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a slur that comes without a definition
stories.head: Define ‘neoliberal’. She couldn’t
body: Among the terms Amit Varma ran through at the end of the episode was ‘neoliberal’, which he called a pure cuss word used against people who are for markets.
At the end of a really great episode of his show *The Seen and the Unseen*, a guest used it. He challenged her on it, and she couldn’t even define it. {107-S10}
It was a slightly awkward bit of conversation, he admitted, and he won’t link the episode. Define the term, he told her, and then they could discuss it: you can’t just use it as a pejorative.

~ Now, whenever he hears someone use the word, his mind stops taking them seriously. {#seriously} He suspects they have been brainwashed in some American university system. “I live in the real world,” he said.
stories.why: If someone cannot define the label they use as an insult, the label is doing their thinking. Asking the other side to define its terms, as Varma did, is where a real argument begins.
